title: Design a game leaderboard
prompt: Design a leaderboard for an online game: players' scores change as they play, and anyone can see the top players and where a given player ranks.

functional: Record a new score for a player.
Return the top N players with their scores.
non_functional: Rank queries stay fast with millions of players.
Scores change frequently, and the ranking reflects a change promptly.
A player's score is not lost when a machine fails.
assumptions: 5,000 rank or top-N reads per second.
A ranking entry, player ID plus score plus overhead, is about 100 bytes.

estimates.label: Memory for the whole ranking
estimates.result: 1 GB, which fits in one machine's memory

estimates.label: Steps for an O(log N) operation

key_points.text: Three operations: submit a score for a player, read the top N, and read one player's rank.
On a Redis sorted set, ZADD against a member already in the set updates its score and position, and ZINCRBY increments a member's score; both are O(log(N)).
ZREVRANGE returns the members within a range of indexes from high score to low, and ZREVRANK returns a member's index ordered by descending scores.
Submit maps to ZADD or ZINCRBY, top N to ZREVRANGE over indexes 0 to N-1, and rank to ZREVRANK plus one, since the index starts at zero.
A sorted set is a collection of unique members ordered by an associated score; members with the same score are ordered lexicographically.
It is implemented with both a skip list and a hash table, so adding an element is O(log(N)) and reading in order needs no further work.
One sorted set per leaderboard, with the player ID as member and the score as score. A durable table keyed by player ID holds the same scores as the record of truth.

notes.text: The leaderboard service writes each score to a durable database and to an in-memory sorted set, and answers rank and top-N reads from the sorted set.
Redis describes sorted sets as suitable when there are tons of updates, with leaderboards as a common use.
Redis Cluster replicates asynchronously, so a write a master has acknowledged can be lost if the master dies before the write reaches its replicas.
That possible loss is the reason for the durable database here: the ranking can be rebuilt from it.

checks.title: Rank and top-N reads are served from an In-memory store
checks.miss: No Connection from a Service to an In-memory store carries the read path.

rationale.text: A sorted set keeps members ordered as they are added, at O(log(N)) per update, so asking for sorted elements needs no further work.

checks.title: Scores are also written to a Database
checks.miss: No Connection from a Service to a Database carries the write path.

rationale.text: Redis Cluster uses asynchronous replication, so there is always a window of time in which it is possible to lose writes.

checks.title: The In-memory store has a replica
checks.miss: There is no In-memory store, or its replication factor is 1.

rationale.text: When a Redis Cluster master fails, one of its replicas is elected and promotes itself to master; the cluster survives partitions in which a majority of masters are reachable and every unreachable master has a reachable replica.

deep_dives.prompt: Why keep the ranking in a sorted set instead of sorting scores when someone asks?

key_points.text: A sorted set holds a skip list and a hash table, and every insert or score update is O(log(N)), so the order is maintained as scores change.
A member's rank is O(log(N)) with ZRANK or ZREVRANK, and a range of M members is O(log(N)+M).
With 10 million players that is about 23 steps per operation, against sorting 10 million scores for each read.

deep_dives.prompt: The in-memory store fails over to a replica. What can happen to recent scores, and how do you recover?

key_points.text: A write may reach a master and be acknowledged without having been propagated to its replicas; if the master then dies, the write is lost.
One replica wins an election and promotes itself to master, and the last elected master's dataset eventually replaces all the other replicas.
So the promoted replica may hold older scores for some players. Because every score also went to the database, the affected entries can be rewritten from it.

deep_dives.prompt: Two players have the same score. In what order do they appear, and how would you rank whoever got there first higher?

key_points.text: Members with the same score are ordered lexicographically by the member string.

With the player ID as member, ties are therefore broken by player ID, which is arbitrary. To favour the earlier achiever, fold the time into what is compared, for example a score that combines points with an inverted timestamp.
